en: The Sūtra on Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Treasury of the Dharma-realm, the sphere of activity of all Buddhas.

In the Great Hall of Merit, adorned with various jewels, he was accompanied by an incalculable multitude of great śrāvakas and great bodhisattvas, as well as an immeasurable assembly of devas, humans, asuras, and others, surrounding him before and behind.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly who manifested in the form of a woman named Guṇavyūhapuṣpā. Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, she rose from her seat, prostrated with her head at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is called a ‘bad friend’ for a bodhisattva, such that a newly trained bodhisattva, having recognized them, should keep far away?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Guṇavairocana, saying:

"I observe that in the world there are no gods, Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas who act as evil friends to a newly initiated bodhisattva regarding unsurpassed bodhi, such as those who delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this so? Because one who is a bodhisattva necessarily seeks unexcelled, perfect enlightenment with diligence for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings;

whereas those who delight in the two vehicles have inferior aspirations, seeking only the bliss of personally realizing parinirvāṇa. For these reasons, a newly trained bodhisattva should not dwell in the same monastery as them, stay in the same room, practice walking meditation in the same place, or travel along the same path.

If there are bodhisattvas who have already attained extensive learning in the Mahāyāna and acquired indestructible faith, I permit you to dwell together with them for the purpose of inspiring their minds toward awakening;

however, if those of such a kind have not yet matured their roots of goodness, you should not preach the Mahāyāna teachings to them, lest they give rise to slander and incur immeasurable transgression.

"A newly initiated bodhisattva should only associate with bodhisattvas who have long studied the Mahāyāna and are well-learned, in order that the roots of goodness planted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment may quickly reach maturity."
One should not associate with those who delight in the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because they obstruct the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva; because they cause one to abandon the bodhicitta; because they cause the bodhicitta to decline; and because they cause one to violate the bodhisattva practices. A bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than abandon the great bodhicitta or give rise to the mental application of seeking the two vehicles.
If a bodhisattva encourages sentient beings to abandon the mind of enlightenment and pursue the stages of the two vehicles;
or if a bodhisattva encourages sentient beings to abandon the mind of enlightenment and commit various evil deeds—in both cases, they shall fall together into hell and undergo intense suffering.

A bodhisattva would rather maintain the great bodhicitta and undergo the sufferings of the hells for committing the five deeds of immediate retribution than ever abandon the great bodhicitta in order to seek the realization of the fruit of a stream-enterer;

a bodhisattva would rather maintain the great bodhicitta and undergo the sufferings of the hells for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas than ever abandon the great bodhicitta in order to seek the realization of the fruit of a once-returner;

a bodhisattva would rather maintain the great bodhicitta and take birth as an animal or become a hungry ghost than ever abandon the great bodhicitta in order to seek the realization of the fruit of a non-returner.

A bodhisattva would rather maintain the great bodhicitta and, having committed the ten non-virtuous actions, fall into the various evil realms, than ever abandon the great bodhicitta while seeking to attain the realization of the fruit of non-arising;

a bodhisattva would rather maintain the great bodhicitta and enter a pit of blazing fire to rescue all sentient beings, than ever abandon the great bodhicitta and, like a cowardly thief, cast themselves into the realm of nirvāṇa.

“Because Bodhisattvas take pity on all sentient beings who wander helplessly through the cycle of birth and death, from the moment they first resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, all devas, humans, asuras, and others should make offerings to them; they have already surpassed the ultimate fruits of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they have already subdued all demonic armies, causing all wicked Māras to be struck with great terror.”
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Guṇavicitrakusuma again entreated the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the ‘army of Māra’?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on me and explain it for me.”
The Buddha told Guṇavairocana:

"If there are those who, upon hearing the teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma, do not give rise to sympathetic joy, do not delight in hearing it, do not seek to enter into its realization, and cannot believe and accept it—instead adding to it derision, mocking, disparagement, contempt, sowing discord, slandering, beating, or expelling them—one should know that such individuals are all the armies of Māra."

These are called those who delight in what is not the Dharma, those of base and inferior nature, those who seek after external paths, those who practice wrong conduct, and those who destroy right view.
You should know that such people slander and revile the Mahāyāna; they shall fall into hell and undergo various intense sufferings.
Once they emerge from there, they will be born among the hungry ghosts, where for hundreds of thousands of kalpas they will constantly consume excrement and filth.

When born again among humans, they will be blind, deaf, mute, or physically deformed; their noses will be flat and crooked, and they will be dull-witted, ignorant, and of stunted or ugly appearance. In this way, as their karmic obstacles gradually dissipate, they will transmigrate through the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may encounter various Buddhas, draw near to them and make offerings, and further hear the Mahāyāna. Having heard it, they may rejoice in it and accept it with faith; because of this, they will give rise to the great bodhicitta, diligently and vigorously cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, and progress step by step toward enlightenment.

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no distinct mental engagement; for the sake of sentient beings, they teach the Dharma of the five vehicles. By the power of their original vows, relying upon the body of the *dharmadhātu*, at all times, from every pore, they spontaneously emit immeasurable rays of Dharma-light and pour down the rain of Dharma with a single sublime voice.
Within a single assembly, for immeasurable sentient beings, those who have long since believed in and delighted in the *śrāvaka* vehicle hear the Buddha preaching the *śrāvaka* vehicle;
those who have long since believed in and delighted in the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle hear the Buddha preaching the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle."
Those who have long since believed in and delighted in the Unsurpassed Vehicle hear the Buddha preach the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
those who have long since believed in and delighted in the various vehicles hear the Buddha preach the Dharma of the various vehicles;
and those who have long since believed in and delighted in the vehicles of humans and devas hear the Buddha preach the Dharma of humans and devas.
Animals, hungry ghosts, and others likewise hear the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma through sounds that accord with their respective types.
If there are those who have not heard the Dharma since time immemorial, they see only the Buddha remaining silent amidst the assembly.

Those who have heard the Mahāyāna and slandered it will fall into the great hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and among gods and humans for immeasurable kalpas. After having fully experienced these sufferings, upon hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma again, they are immediately able to rejoice in it and give rise to deep, pure faith, thereby awakening the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Guṇavairocana Puṣpa again entreated the Buddha, saying:
"What is called the Mahāyāna?
By what meaning is this Mahāyāna designated?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Since you are able to delight in hearing the merits of the Mahāyāna, listen closely, listen closely!"
Reflect upon this well; I shall now analyze and explain for you the various meanings denoted by the name of this Mahāyāna.
This vehicle comprehensively encompasses and guides all things in a vast and far-reaching manner without omission; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
The merit of this vehicle is profoundly deep and its subtlety exceeds all measure and calculation; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is firm and solid; because false conceptualization cannot shake it, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is true and real; because it extends to the end of the future without exhaustion, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is vast and empty; because it encompasses the entire dharma-realm and reaches infinitely beyond all bounds, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like the ocean, swallowing and accumulating a treasury of jewels of merit; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like a mountain, acting as a bulwark for the region so that heterodox followers do not disturb it; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like space, encompassing all categories of sentient and non-sentient beings; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like the earth, for it can universally cause the growth of mundane and supramundane virtues; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like water, for it moistens all equally so that none may wither; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like fire, for it incinerates all hindrances so that no residual habits remain; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like the wind, sweeping away all the clouds and mists of birth and death; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like the sun, illuminating all categories of beings and bringing them to maturity; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is like the moon, able to remove the heat of affliction and destroy all false darkness; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is noble and honored, revered by the eight classes of devas and nāgas; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is constantly extolled and praised in song by the gandharvas; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is constantly saluted, venerated, and respected by the Four Heavenly Kings, Brahmā, and Śakra; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is constantly honored and guarded by all the nāgas, devas, and others; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is constantly and diligently studied by all bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle sustains the noble lineage of all buddhas, causing it to flourish and increase from one to another; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because it is perfect and endowed with great majesty that outshines all others;
this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because it provides for all sentient beings universally so that none lack anything;
this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because its power is like a medicinal tree that cures all ailments.
This vehicle can destroy all the thieves of affliction belonging to sentient beings; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle can turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to benefit all; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is subtle, profound, and secret, such that it cannot be fully expounded; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle employs divine power to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it may never be severed;
therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna. This vehicle can manifest the ultimate principles of both the conventional and the ultimate truths;
therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna. This vehicle can manifest all the practices of the bodhisattvas without exception; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because it can manifest all the qualities of the Buddha-ground without exception;
this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because it brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings throughout the limits of the future;
this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna because its ultimate capacity establishes great significance with inexhaustible sublime functions.
This vehicle is profound and subtle; those with inferior inclinations cannot believe or accept it, and thus it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is impartial; only those with superior inclinations can believe and accept it, and thus it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is vast; the ignorant and foolish cannot fathom it and instead treat it with derision and laughter, and thus it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle is noble and sublime; because it can be realized by superior wisdom and is constantly cherished and played with [as a jewel], it is called the Mahāyāna.
This vehicle transcends the Pratyekabuddhayāna and others, being supreme and peerless; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.

When the Buddha had thus spoken on the names, meanings, essences, functions, and the preeminent merits of this Mahāyāna, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial musical instruments in the sky resounded spontaneously without being struck; and exquisite celestial flowers fell in profusion and confusion. Immeasurable devaputras and countless śrāvakas, hearing this Dharma-sound and beholding these auspicious omens, all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Simultaneously, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of newly initiated bodhisattvas realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Dharma-gate is most rare; it is able to universally benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings. By what name should it be upheld and disseminated?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sūtra is named 'Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna,' and it is also named 'Expounding the Karmic Obstructions of Slandering the Dharma. You should uphold it by these names."

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda and the other immeasurable śrāvakas, the countless bodhisattvas such as Guṇavyūha and Puṣpaśrī, along with the entire great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
